tieu_de: Why Losing $100 Hurts More Than Winning $100

canh._ghi_chu: GIỮ CHÂN: mở vòng lặp (trả lời ở c019)

tham_so.loi: Why does losing $100 hurt more than winning $100 feels good?
tham_so.loi_doc: Why does losing a hundred dollars hurt more than winning a hundred dollars feels good?

tham_so.loi: Max found out the hard way, with his very first stocks.
The pain of losing felt about twice as strong as the joy.

canh._ghi_chu: GIỮ CHÂN: hứa trả lời sau (c016–c017)

tham_so.loi: And it made him do something strange. We'll get there.
Three months earlier, Max had saved two thousand dollars.
He split it between two stocks. Let's call them Green and Red.
Like most of us, Max thought he was a calm, logical investor.

canh._ghi_chu: GIỮ CHÂN: câu báo trước (~25–30 s)

tham_so.loi: He didn't know it yet, but his brain had already picked a side.
And the same thing happens to you, every time money is on the line.
A month later, Green was up twenty percent.
Max felt like a genius. He sold it right away and locked in the win.
Red, on the other hand, was down twenty percent.
Part of him said sell. Another part said wait, it will come back.
So he waited. And he waited some more.
Online, everyone said Red was about to bounce back.
Six months later, Red was down forty percent.
He sold his winner too early, and held his loser far too long.

canh._ghi_chu: GIỮ CHÂN: câu hỏi thẳng người xem

tham_so.loi: Why would a smart person do that? Be honest. Have you done it too?
Psychologists have a name for this feeling. It's called loss aversion.
tham_so.dinh_nghia: Losses hurt more than gains feel good

tham_so.loi: Picture two moments. Winning one hundred dollars, and losing one hundred dollars.
Same amount of money. But the loss weighs a lot more, like a tilted scale.
Selling a loser means admitting the loss is real.
Holding it lets you pretend it's only a loss on paper.
When investors do this with stocks, it has its own name: the disposition effect.
tham_so.dinh_nghia: Sell winners early, hold losers long

tham_so.loi: In 1979, Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky studied how people choose between risky bets.
tham_so.loi_doc: In nineteen seventy-nine, Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky studied how people choose between risky bets.

tham_so.loi: Here's a classic bet. Flip a coin. Heads, you win $150. Tails, you lose $100.
tham_so.loi_doc: Here's a classic bet. Flip a coin. Heads, you win a hundred and fifty dollars. Tails, you lose a hundred dollars.

canh._ghi_chu: GIỮ CHÂN: mời đoán trước khi nói kết quả

tham_so.loi: Would you take it? Think about it for a second.
The odds favor you. Yet in tests like this, many people say no.
In 1992, they estimated that losses weigh about twice as much as gains.
tham_so.loi_doc: In nineteen ninety-two, they estimated that losses weigh about twice as much as gains.

tham_so.loi: Their typical estimate was about two point two five.
In 1998, Terrance Odean looked at thousands of real trading accounts.
tham_so.loi_doc: In nineteen ninety-eight, Terrance Odean looked at thousands of real trading accounts.

tham_so.loi: Investors sold winners more readily than losers. Just like Max.
Fair warning: newer studies suggest the effect is smaller in some everyday choices.
A year later, Max faces the same choice again.
This time, he notices the little voice that says wait.

canh._ghi_chu: GIỮ CHÂN: đổi nhịp — Max nhận ra

tham_so.loi: He asks one question: would I buy this stock today?
The answer is no. So he sells, and moves on.
Here are three ways to keep loss aversion from running your money.
Tip one: ask if you would buy it today, at today's price.
Tip two: decide when you will sell before you buy.
Write it down. Future you will thank you.
Tip three: check your portfolio less often.
Shlomo Benartzi and Richard Thaler argued that checking often makes loss-averse investors fear stocks more.
Daily checks show many red days. Yearly checks show the bigger picture.
So: losses feel bigger, we hold losers too long, and simple rules help.
Max still feels the sting of a loss. He just doesn't let it decide anymore.
